why: Pass 1 enumerated 9 screens as the coverage denominator.
Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: The empty inbox is an empty rectangle
finding.detail: `inbox.jsx` renders `<List items={data} />` whenever data resolves, including when it resolves to zero rows. A brand-new account therefore lands on a bordered rectangle with a header and nothing else — no explanation that the account is genuinely empty rather than broken, and no action.
finding.recommendation: Branch on `data.length === 0` and render a state that says the inbox is empty, why that is expected on a new account, and the one action that changes it.

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: Loading replaces the whole layout with a spinner
finding.detail: `if (!data) return <Spinner />` throws away the chrome the reader was already looking at. The header, the toolbar and the list frame all vanish and then reappear, so every navigation costs a full-page flash even when the payload is small.
finding.recommendation: Keep the frame mounted and render row skeletons inside it, so only the rows change and nothing the reader is looking at moves.

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: Row density is not tuned for the long case
finding.detail: The list uses one spacing value for every row, which reads comfortably at twenty messages and becomes an enormous scroll at two thousand. There is no compact affordance and no grouping by date.
finding.recommendation: Add a compact row height and group rows under sticky date headers so the long case stays navigable.

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: Errors surface the raw HTTP status
finding.detail:
`return
{error.status}
` puts the literal number in front of the reader. A 403 on a shared thread and a 500 on a broken server are the same experience: a bare number, no explanation of whether the message is gone, private, or merely unavailable right now, and nothing to click.
finding.recommendation: Map the status to a sentence that says what happened, whether anything was lost, and the single action that resolves it — retry, request access, or go back to the inbox.

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: No visible focus ring on the reply affordance
finding.detail: The reply control is styled from scratch and never restores an outline on `:focus-visible`, so a keyboard reader tabbing through a long thread loses their place entirely once they pass the message body.
finding.recommendation: Restore a `:focus-visible` outline with a 2px offset on every interactive element that overrides the default.

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: Nothing signals that a draft was saved
finding.detail: Compose autosaves, but the interface never says so. The reader has no way to distinguish work that is safe from work that is about to be lost, which is the single highest-stakes uncertainty on the screen.
finding.recommendation: Show a quiet, timestamped 'Saved' marker that updates on each autosave and turns into an explicit warning when a save fails.

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: Send is irreversible the instant it is pressed
finding.detail: There is no undo window. The most consequential and most frequently regretted action in the product commits immediately, and the only recovery is a second message apologising for the first.
finding.recommendation: Hold the send for a few seconds behind an 'Undo' snackbar, the way every mail client the reader already uses does.

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: Preference changes give no confirmation
finding.detail: Toggles write on change and render nothing back. The reader flips a switch and is left to infer from the absence of an error that the preference stuck.
finding.recommendation: Reflect the saved state on the control itself and surface failures inline next to the toggle that failed.

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: Every section carries identical visual weight
finding.detail: Account, notifications, appearance and the destructive account-deletion block are all rendered as the same flat list of rows, so the one irreversible action on the screen is as quiet as a theme preference.
finding.recommendation: Give the destructive block its own separated, differently-weighted treatment at the end of the page.

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: A search with no matches looks like a failure
finding.detail: Zero results renders the same bare list frame as an error, so the reader cannot tell whether the query genuinely matched nothing or whether the search itself broke.
finding.recommendation: Say that the query matched nothing, echo the query back, and offer the obvious relaxation — drop a filter, search all mail.

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: Results arrive with no transition
finding.detail: Each keystroke swaps the result list instantly, so the list flickers through intermediate states while the reader is still typing.
finding.recommendation: Debounce the query and cross-fade the result set so the change reads as one settled update.

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: Archive is a second inbox with no way back
finding.detail: The archive reuses the inbox list wholesale, including its row actions, but offers no un-archive affordance. Filing something away is therefore a one-way door reachable by a single click.
finding.recommendation: Give archived rows a restore action, and make the archive's header visually distinct from the inbox's so the two are never confused.

why: Pass 1 appraisal against the lens rubric.

finding.title: The list does not reflow below 640px
finding.detail: The row lays sender, subject, preview and timestamp on one line with fixed columns, so on a narrow viewport the subject truncates to a few characters while the timestamp keeps its full width.
finding.recommendation: Stack sender and timestamp on one line and give subject and preview the full width below it under 640px.

why: Four screens fail the same way for the same reason. Filed as one systemic finding so the plan orders it as one piece of work rather than four unrelated tickets.

finding.title: Absence is unhandled product-wide, not screen by screen
finding.detail: Inbox, search, archive and drafts each render only their success case. There is no shared empty-state component and no convention for what absence looks like, so every screen invents its own or, more often, invents nothing. Fixing these one at a time will produce four different empty states.
finding.recommendation: Build one empty-state component that takes a headline, an explanation and a primary action, then adopt it everywhere absence is possible.

why: The column read across the six graded screens surfaced a gap that no single-screen appraisal could see.

finding.title: Error handling exists on exactly one screen
finding.detail: Thread is the only screen that checks `error` at all, and it does so badly. The other five destructure `error` and never read it, so a failed request on any of them leaves the spinner up forever. The reader waits indefinitely for a request that has already failed.
finding.recommendation: Handle the error branch on every screen that fetches, and make an unresolved request time out into an error rather than an eternal spinner.

why: Reach times stakes times recoverability ranks this first in the set: thread is the screen reached from a shared link by someone who has no other route in, and a bare status code gives them nothing to act on.
